utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Would you please read the affirmation that's shown to you now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Please sit down. Mr. Djordjevic has some questions for you. Yes, Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. Would you please give us your name.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: My name is Zoran Stankovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, your date and place of birth.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: I was born on the 9th of November, 1954, in the village of Tegoviste of Vladicin Han municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Tell us, what is your occupation?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm a -- I'm a specialist in forensic medicine, and I work in the field of forensic medicine and I teach at the medical school.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Tell us about your current work status.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm now vice dean at the academy in Novi Sad, and I also teach at the dental school in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: All right. To avoid me putting a lot of questions to you, would you please freely describe your education and your career up-to-date.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: Upon completing my elementary school or high school and medical school at the university, I first served my military service as a resident physician, following which I became an active member of the Yugoslav People's Army. I first served in the rank of lieutenant, I served in Nis, following which I was sent to the garrison in Pec, in Kosovo. After that I was given a residency training in the field of forensic medicine in Belgrade at the military medical academy in Belgrade, where I remained after completing my residency training and becoming specialist. As an officer of the medical corps I reached the rank of major-general, and I headed the highest medical institution within the JNA and the Yugoslav Army after that, currently the Army of Serbia. And after leaving that office I served as minister of defence for a period of six months in the state union of Serbia and Montenegro -- or rather, I remained in that position for a year and a half. What I can say is that I defended my doctoral thesis at the military medical academy, and my topic was autopsy of corpses in war conditions, and I examined in the course of that 1.360 corpses using 20 variables, and I wrote doctoral thesis on that topic of about 860 pages. What is important in my work and what I want to highlight is that from the beginning of armed conflict in the territory of the former Yugoslavia I worked as a volunteer performing autopsies on corpses in the theatre of war. And in the course of that, I performed autopsies on about 5.000 corpses. I worked on mass graves in the territory of the entire former Yugoslavia. The first large mass grave that I worked on was in Vukovar. I performed autopsy on all the victims in Vukovar. I headed the medical team working there. And as new mass graves were uncovered and as the number of victims grew, I worked more and more. In Croatia, in addition to Vukovar, I also worked in Gospic, in Tenja, in Binaj near Osijek. I also worked in Knin, in Oranica [phoen], and some other places. As for Bosnia, I worked in the entire area of Eastern Bosnia, Zvornik, Kravice, Srebrenica, Vlasenica, Sarajevo, Ugljevik, Brcko, and some other locations. I also worked in Herzegovina, in Bileca, Nevesinje, Trebinje, and so on. During my work there I was also a member of the federal committee on gathering evidence on violations of international humanitarian law up -- this was starting from 1993 and from 2002 until 2004 I served as chairman of that committee. While performing that work I met frequently with the representatives of the ICTY. My first meeting with them was in 1992 and in 1993 with the first chairman of the committee for war crimes, Carsten Hoffman. I also met Cherif Bassiouni, Richard Goldstone, Louise Arbour, and Carla del Ponte. I met with them both here in The Hague and in Belgrade. In addition to that, I wrote some 30 papers about my work and activities in this field. I was also an invited speaker in the parliaments of Great Britain and parliament of Ukraine as well as in various other institutions in London, Cambridge, Paris, Budapest. I was invited to come and give lectures in The Hague, Amsterdam, and Utrecht, and this has been part of my work until today.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much for this exhaustive answer, Doctor. I have to say that the Defence following the latest Court order did some corrections on the expert report of Dr. Stankovic, which is entitled: "Findings and opinion of the medical examiners who performed the autopsies of the bodies found in Kosovo and Metohija and elsewhere," and the work of experts who took part in the forensic examination of the sites where the bodies were found. In the case IT-05-87/1-T, Prosecutor versus Vlastimir Djordjevic, this redacted document is marked as D011-5432. Now, please tell me, did you write this report, and is this your expert witness report?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This redacted version of your report will be offered to be admitted into evidence, and I assume that that will be done after you complete your testimony. But if the Chamber considers that this redacted report can be admitted into evidence immediately, now, then I will make my suggestion accordingly to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Of course we would contemplate, Mr. Djordjevic, is that if the doctor confirms the report is his subject to the deletion of the two or three passages we've identified because there's been no factual foundation for those parts in the evidence before us, we would suggest you put the report to the doctor and we will receive it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was the intention of the Defence. Thank you, Your Honour. We will be first examining Exhibit P1167, so I will ask to see page 9 of this exhibit, page 9 in B/C/S and page 10 in English. As far as I can he see, this is in German. We need P1167, page 10 in the English version. Do we have the German version -- all right. Now this is good.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, P1167 is a report by experts from Austria who examined Kacanik and Kotlina sites in Kosovo. We also know, however, that experts from Switzerland participated in this work. Could you please comment on this part of the report. First of all, tell us whether you are familiar with what is stated here; and if so, would you please give us your comment on the methodology of work of the Swiss experts.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: As you know, all work, especially work of specialists, has an appropriate methodology and has rules that need to be followed in the course of that work. In this particular case there are differences in the approach when processing the corpses from the point of view of forensic medicine. However, there are different schools. There's English school, American school of thought, Russian school of thought, and they're not contradictory. But when it comes to autopsying corpses, bodies need to be examined in a generally accepted way, which is to say that the written record of that autopsy needs to contain certain elements such as height, muscular development, development of the skeleton. The body needs to be described, its appearance, eyes, hair, teeth, and so on. Following that, the written record needs to reflect the injuries that are on the body as well as any peculiar elements that can be used for identification, such as scars, moles, and so on. Following that, they need to examine all cavities, all body cavities, and then they need to describe clothing, damage, any biological traces on the clothing. And then if autopsy is performed they also need to describe the findings of the internal examination. Then needs to follow a conclusion on the cause of death, was it a natural or violent death, was it an accident, suicide or murder. Then is the death linked to the injuries found on the bodies. Then the injuries need to be described, giving some ideas as to what caused those injuries, what kind of object. And then they need to make a conclusion in that written finding, make photographs. Photographs need to reflect all elements, clothing, body, all injuries need to be photographed so that, as in this case, somebody could perform an additional analysis and give their opinion on the first autopsy performed. What we can see in this report of Austrian experts is that these autopsy records, written records, cannot provide almost any kind of information to the Court. If we take the report for corpse number 2, Izija Loku it says there when it comes to injuries the following: "Traces caused by explosion and fire were found on the body. Skull was completely smashed." And then they finish by saying: "The traces on the body caused by explosion could have been caused during life or after death of the victim." I don't think that anybody can make any sort of a valid conclusion based on this meager information contained in this report. When speaking of mass graves that I worked on, I worked on them during combat operations at the front line between the two warring sides. But when somebody works for an institution such as the ICTY and has all the logistical support, that is to say both adequate funding, adequate personnel, and technical equipment needed, then it is unacceptable for that person to provide such a report which is superficial and to treat an autopsy of a body in such a superficial manner. Let me add one more thing. When one makes an analysis, say in the case of Izijah Loku, all we can -- all we have is this paper about his autopsy, which contains only two sentences about the injuries and doesn't even give an opinion as to whether these injuries were inflicted during life or after death of the person.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now see page 12 of this document in B/C/S, and let's have page 12 in English as well. We might need to see page 13 also at some point.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: We see autopsy report for corpse number 4, Kuqi Xhemajl. Could you please comment on this report.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: Autopsy report and findings contained therein again are contradictory. In the first part of the report it says that: "To the right of the spine on the back there was one injury visible, most likely caused by a fire-arm." And then the same doctor, Markwalder, concludes that there were traces of explosion and fire-arm and that superficial wounds could be seen on the back. So on one hand they're saying that this was a fire-arm injury, and on the other hand they're claiming that this was an injury caused by an explosion. From the point of view of forensic medicine, that is completely unacceptable, and it is up to the Trial Chamber to evaluate this.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now go back to page 7 in B/C/S and also page 7 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: There is a description of traces found at the scene of crime in Rastani and traces of projectiles and so on and so forth. What are the obligations of your profession vis-a-vis this type of information? What is this all about, as a matter of fact?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: During my time as today in Serbia there was a military term, you would be mobilised, and in such circumstances certain army members could also get killed. When such cases occurred, then an investigating judge of the military court would call in a forensic medical expert to form part of the team. His or her obligation was during all investigative measures to carry out the registering of all biological traces at the scene of crime or where the body was found and its environs. In such circumstances, my role was that after, say, a spent cartridge was found or an instrument for which it is believed was used to cause death, my task was to investigate it, describe the scene, and seal the object in question, to send it to the lab which would then examine it for any other further traces. On page 7 it is stated that the incline on which the event took place is thickly overgrown. There were many conifer trees there. In such circumstances those who were in attendance of the scene had to have examined the foliage and the leaves for any blood traces, tissue traces, or other biological traces, for example, parts of bones or hair. Since in such locations when there is -- when bullets are used and fire-arms, then such traces are frequently found. This, however, was not described, which may mean that there may have been some traces or there may not have been some traces. In any case, it is clear that they did not register any traces of projectile impact resulting from this description, and they didn't find any biological traces. That's why I made this conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: So what was the conclusion?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: The conclusion I could provide from my forensic medical point of view without going into the realm of the judiciary, my conclusion would be that there were no executions at such a location or this location.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On the same page there is a description which states that clothes covered in soot were found close to the well shaft. Can you tell us anything more about such traces, how could they be in such a location and can that serve as an indication to show that the bodies had previously been burned?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: The bodies were burned there. In -- had the bodies been burned there, apart from soot traces, we would have found carbonised part of human bodies. They were not, however, and the conclusion is that the bodies were brought in from another location and then thrown down the well shaft. In the process of the bodies being moved, given that there were traces of flames visible on the bodies, the clothing particles referred to fell off the bodies and some of them ended up close to the well shaft.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 7 we can speak of certain material traces of biological origin and their contamination or destruction. However, we can see the same thing on page 16, which is 17 in the B/C/S -- actually, it's the same page in the English. Before providing your answer I would just kindly wait for page 16 in the B/C/S and 17 in English. I would like to hear some of your observations concerning what I have just said and what we can see on the screen.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: As I've already stated, an investigation must be carried out according to certain procedure prescribed by the law. In our country it is the Law on Criminal Procedure. The person in charge of the investigation is an investigating judge. Under the law in Serbia, although in comparison to some other countries' legislations, we he will also see certain amendments to that law. It seems that the villagers, without the presence of any competent authorities, began to clear those wells and extract material from it, thus destroying important evidence. They did this before the investigating team arrived, which is what we can see on page 7. Although later on the team was there, they still continued doing this by themselves without any monitoring or objections by the investigating team. It is clear that it took place on the 11th of September, 1999, at 10.00. From our point of view, this is unacceptable.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. My next question is dealt with on pages --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By the Chamber's leave, and I wanted to have something on the record, I wanted to say as follows, also for ease of reference for my Prosecution colleagues. At page 8 in the B/C/S and English and then page 101 and 102 in the B/C/S and page 75 and 76 in the English as well as at page 106 in the B/C/S, which is page 80 in the English, there is mention made of a number of registered fire-arm wounds as well as a number of cartridges found at the location. Could we please see page 8 of the document in the B/C/S and 8 in the English to illustrate that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Everything I've discussed so far is on the other pages I referred to and is also contained on page 8. Could you please comment.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: When one looks at all fire-arm wounds described on the bodies, it seems that all those bodies which were pulled out of the well or exhumed, there were 26 fire-arm wounds described in total on those bodies. One needs to bear in mind that most of the bodies were destroyed and many parts missing. This makes me conclude that a possible number of fire-arm wounds or gun-shot wounds were far higher, although only 12 cartridges were found. In addition to that, in the upper well shaft ten cartridges were found, which when analysed by ballistic experts were found to have been fired from a single fire-arm, meaning that there was a single person firing those shots. And the number of registered gun-shot wounds far exceeds that figure by 14. This is another proof, in my view, that those gun-shot wounds were caused or inflicted in a different location other than the location where the bodies were found.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we go to page 9 in both versions. For ease of reference I also wanted to refer to page 34 in the B/C/S and 35 in the English as well as page 35 in the B/C/S and page 36 in the English and page 36 in the B/C/S and page 37 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I wanted to hear your opinion, Professor, concerning the position of the mortal remains found in the well. In your expert report, and as we can see from these descriptions, that there were different levels at which the mortal remains were found.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: During the exhumation process the people involved, the experts, that is, they also described at which depth they found the body parts. It seems that on the surface only small body parts were found, such as pieces of bones and tissue as well as partially carbonised items of -- pieces of clothing. The same type of traces was found in the bottom-most layer, which indicates that the bodies and the remains were found in other locations, and as they were found they were thrown in the well. Had the bodies been thrown in first and then explosives later, then on the surface level we would have had these small body particles, whereas in the lower levels we would still have larger parts and bodies better preserved than described here. If we look at this we also have small particles on the surface and at the bottom of the well as well as in between.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction:

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And in between we have a different situation which does not prove the explosion thesis.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please go to page 13 in the B/C/S and in the English. The same topic is covered on page 14 in both versions, as well as page 23 in the B/C/S and 23 in the English. Then page 24 in the B/C/S and 24 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: My first question has to do with the location of explosive or blast injuries on the corpse number 5 described here. This is page 13 in both versions as well as 14. Could I please have your comment concerning these injuries on the corpse number 5.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: In the description of the position of the body when found during the exhumation process by the experts, it is stated that the body was lying on its stomach which means that that is how it was put inside the well. Next we have a description stating that the centre of the explosion took place in the abdominal region. What does it mean? If the body had been thrown into the well and lying on its stomach against the soil, and then after that there was an explosive device inserted into the well, be it a hand-grenade, an explosive, then it would have been realistic to expect that such blast injuries would be found on the back, not in the abdominal region because the explosion could not have destroyed the abdominal region since the abdominal region was lying flat on the ground and thus protected. Therefore, that injury could not have been caused when the body was already in the well. The same goes for bodies number 12, for example, which is also lying on its stomach and the blast injuries are on the front of the thoracic region. Then body number 13 lying on the stomach, and the blast injury was in the left armpit. This is another proof that these blast injuries did not occur in the well but elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I have already provided all the references, so I won't go through them again. My next question is this: What does the intensity of injuries in bodies number 5, 6, 8, and 9, as well as 10 and 21 indicate to you in relation to the number of metal fragments found in the well?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The reference is page 106. Could it be placed on the monitor, as well as page 80 in the English. 106 in the B/C/S and 80 in the English. Let us wait for that first.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The bodies you referred to had extensive destructive injuries caused by mines or explosives. For example, corpse number 5 only had the torso and the arms, whereas the lower extremities are completely missing. Body number 6 is missing both legs. Body number 8 has most of it -- of the body missing. In the well, however, only 16 metal fragments were found. Having in mind that the expert teams had metal detecters and that they extracted all those 16 metal fragments from the soil, one can say with a large degree of certainty that such a small number of metal fragments disproves the thesis that these destructive injuries were caused in the well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we please have page 16 in the B/C/S as well as in the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: This has to do with item 10 of your report. This has to do with the possible mechanisms of skull fractures in the corpses found in the well. The first reference, page 16 refers to corpse number 7, then we have corpse number 16 which is page 29 in both versions, however, we don't need to see that. Please just provide us with your general answer concerning these two examples.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: During the autopsy of this body only one injury mechanism was concerned -- was explained concerning the skull. It is stated that the skull had been fractured by a blunt instrument. However, having in mind the type of soil in which there was all -- there were also rocks and that there were other bodies in the well, one cannot exclude the possibility that after such a fall - and we know that the well was between 8 and 10 metres deep - that the bodies when they fell from such a height hit a hard, blunt surface which contained rocks or other solid body parts such as the skull of another body or the knee. It is possible that in such cases too there are injuries to the skull bones. Therefore, one must not exclude that possibility either as a possible mechanism of injuries.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the transcript I think I said that the corpse number 16 is on page 29 in the B/C/S and English page 26. Page 16 in the B/C/S and in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: We have descriptions of body parts of a single corpse it seems which were found at different depths. The different depths -- well, you have provided us with your conclusion when you said that there was a possibility that the bodies were brought from elsewhere. However, when discussing these depths you said that the corpses were practically not extracted but exhumed from the wells, which indicates that the wells were filled up. Can you comment briefly on the location where those wells were. Would one usually expect to find such wells in such a location?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: That question goes outside of the scope of my work. I can give you an answer as a person who grew up in a rural area.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: In that case, I withdraw my question. I will not require you to answer. Now, tell me, please, what does the finding of gun-shot and penetrating wounds in body number 11 indicate?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We need page 21 in the B/C/S and page 22 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: But we can see the same material on the following two pages, 22 in B/C/S and 23 in English.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: My experience in finding in one body various injuries which were inflicted with different objects such as gun-shot wounds and injuries from mines and explosives, then that indicates that such injuries could have been inflicted and most likely were inflicted during armed conflict between warring sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 26 in B/C/S and page 27 in English, the same document. Could we see it on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Doctor, we're dealing now with body number 14 here. It says here that there was a bandage on the right leg. Can you comment on that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the presence of a bandage on the right leg indicates that the injury was inflicted before the death came about and that the injury was inflicted at another location and that first aid was provided by putting a bandage on the injured part.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now see page 30 in B/C/S and 31 in English. The reference for my question can be found on the following pages too, 31 and 32.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: If the workers performing autopsy had metal detecters - and we know that they did have them - could they have established whether the injuries on, say, corpse number 19 were inflicted by explosive devices or by conventional fire-arms?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: In my objections to the work of the Austrian team I stated that some things were not clear to me. In this particular case, what I find objectionable is that despite having metal detecter the expert team could not establish whether gun-shot wounds on the front part of the abdomen were a result of mines and explosives or were a result from projectiles fired by -- from fire-arms. It is also not clear to me, despite the fact that the body was severely decomposed, it also surprises me that they couldn't establish whether the injuries were inflicted during the life or after death. And this is what makes the conclusion so difficult. If the injuries were inflicted by gun-shot firing, then they could be either penetrating wounds or some other kinds of wounds; whereas, if they were inflicted by explosives then most likely fragments would be still found in the body. Metal detecter, if it is properly used, could dispel this dilemma. And this is why I think that this finding is objectionable, unacceptable, and it reflects a very superficial attitude toward work.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, we as laymen are also interested in learning the following. Had you been there and had you had a metal detecter, how would you have established whether injuries were caused by mines and explosives and shrapnels or by fire-arms? How would that look in practice, your work?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, what you do is you take a knife, you open up abdominal cavity, and then by palpitation and by establishing damage to organs within the abdominal cavity - and in this case we can see that liver was damaged and also heart - we would by this physical examination look for shrapnel. And according to our Law on Criminal Procedure, it is also the duty of a person performing autopsy when finding any shrapnel or any particles of mines and explosive to extract them and to turn them over together with the body remains and any written findings and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we now see page 34 of this document in B/C/S and also page 34 in English. The relevant English text can be found also on page 35. We are now dealing with corpse number 22.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, we can see the findings of your colleagues from the Austrian team, and I would like to hear your opinion about their findings.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: I can say that I can accept the part of the finding which says that in the windpipe no soot particles were found, that is to say traces of gun-shots while people were still alive. That means that while they were still alive they didn't breathe in any fumes. That is to say that the gun-shot wounds were inflicted after death.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: After death. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see page 32 and 33 in B/C/S -- or rather, just 32 on the monitor, please. And this same page in English. The relevant material can also be found on the following page.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: This is corpse number 20. Again we see the conclusion -- the finding by your colleagues about the object that inflicted injuries. Can you comment on this, please.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: In the description of injuries on corpse number 20, the autopsy experts stated that on the back there were several shrapnel wounds and that they also found an injury caused by a sharp object, a knife wound, on the left side of the neck. Examination established that this injury did not damage any arteries. Sometimes, given that shrapnel has uneven surface, that it is made out of steel, and that it is also sharp, injuries caused by shrapnel can resemble knife wounds, knife injuries. Therefore, given the appearance and description of this wound, I believe that most likely this injury was also caused by one of the shrapnels because if somebody had wanted to torture this victim they wouldn't have stopped at just one knife stab. This is the experience I have after having performed all those autopsies. So they wouldn't have stopped at just one knife stab that didn't damage any arteries. It is just unlikely.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: I have to say that in cases where there are very few injuries on the body, as is the case of corpse of Zymer Loku, and when you see that this is an elderly person, this particular victim was born in 1932, and if you have an injury which in order to have caused the death needed to be described in more elaborate terms, then one can conclude that autopsy experts found only one penetrating gun-shot wound on the right leg, on the right calf. utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see page 38 in B/C/S, or rather, there's parts that's relevant on page 39 too. And could we see 39 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: And please take this into account when giving answers to my following questions, Doctor.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, I will ask for page 5 in B/C/S to be shown on the screen. That's 65 ter 00383, and we need page 5 in B/C/S and page 56 in English. My question has to do with the following. Page 5 in B/C/S, please, and page 56 in English. We see the first page in English version of the document. I see that we still cannot see page 56 in English. It's obvious that we have some problems with e-court. 65 ter 00383, page 5 in B/C/S and page 56 in English, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: All right. I will ask the question anyway, and later on we can come back to this so as not to lose any time. The question will be short. Is it possible to establish the cause of death in persons whose mortal remains were about two months in water?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: The cause of death of persons whose mortal remains were in water for two months cannot be established by autopsy alone. To establish what happened before death includes a number of measures that have to be taken by investigation organs in order to find out whether they drowned or whether they were put in water after death. In this case, without -- without any doubt, they established that these persons were drowned while alive, but there was nothing to support this claim.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If the mortal remains have been in water for two or two and a half months, can one find fresh traces of blood on them? That would be my next question.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: It is generally known that depending on the conditions, but after death blood begins to decompose, and after two months in water it is certainly not possible to establish that there is any presence of red blood on the opening of the vulva. One can say that this is putrefying liquid, but not that there is any presence of blood. At the same time, if someone says that because of the decomposition changes it is impossible to establish the existence of a wound, then one could ask: Well, how is it then possible to see traces of blood when we know that blood decomposes very quickly, particularly in water, and then not to register injuries? So I think that a claim like this cannot be defended in any way.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see that finally we have the English version. This question is connected with page 5 in B/C/S and page 56 in the English version, as well as page 8 in the B/C/S version and page 58 in the English version. And in this particular case the persons who carried out autopsy did not describe this. And the -- nor was there such a description in some other female bodies that were taken out of the water.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: And could we see such markings on the underwear after a body had been two or two and a half months in water?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The next page of this document is page 8 in B/C/S, that is to say page 56 of the English version. The body is marked SIP1C2. Can you please comment on the injuries registered on this body and give us your opinion about the cause of injuries on this body.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, in the case of this woman, injuries that were registered were injuries to the right inner thigh, abrasive ones, that could be the consequence of trying to jump over an edge of a well. It also could be the consequence of the fall and hitting some object or the body of another person who could have been in the well. So that's more or less everything I could say at this moment. I might add something later.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Let us now look at page 17 in B/C/S and page 64 in English. My colleague tells me that the transcript says this was a body marked SIP1C4, so it was actually SIP1C1, that's the body described on page 4 before what we talked about now. utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Would that be possible after so much time, Professor?

utterances.text: On page 30 and on page --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before the witness enters, Your Honour, I wanted to say the page 17 in the B/C/S and 64 in the English is the correct reference. We can deal with that before the witness enters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I believe we have the right page now.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Concerning our last topic, which was the fracture of ribs, this is what you addressed as well as the possible mechanisms of rib fractures with these two persons. Is there anything you wished to add?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: I can only reiterate what I have already said.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Please go ahead because we were interrupted, and there were certain things that were not clear.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: In the summary the French experts say that the thoracic fractures were ante mortem without skin injuries, which seem to indicate that there was a lot of pressure exerted on the body before it was thrown into the well and the injuries were the cause of the body being pressed against the coping of the well. However, this is not reflected in the conclusions because in the conclusions of the autopsy for SIPC3C they say there were lateral fractures to the thorax created ante mortem caused by a fall. They concluded that the ribs were fractured because the body was pressed against the coping of the well before it was thrown down the well; whereas, in the autopsy findings we have them listed as the result of the fall. This is the contradiction. Also, I can say that rib fractures can be created in both the ways described in the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Concerning the injuries of these corpses, what kind of injuries can one expect to see when a body falls into a well? Perhaps you could be more specific, say for rib fractures.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: First of all, if we have in mind the description of the well, which was inspected, and if we know that the diameter of the well was 1.10 metres, which is 110 centimetres, and that it had a wooden fence, and that the other well was 105 centimetres with a concrete wall around it, and the third well had the diameter of 100 centimetres with a wooden fence; in such circumstances it would be realistic to expect a larger number of injuries on the bodies than those described if the bodies had been thrown into the well head first, as is stated on page 31 of the translation. It is realistic to expect that if one throws a body down the well it goes down under a slanted angle, which means that it is very likely that the head would hit a wall of the shaft, creating injuries such as abrasions, skull fractures with damage to the brain tissue which may result in death. In -- among these cases we do see one such injury on one body, but not on the others. It is realistic to expect that if a person is falling head first, that that person would instinctively spread out arms or spread the legs, thus changing the position of the body. And at such protruded parts of the body, such as the limbs, some injuries should be registered; however, we do not see that save for the two abrasions of the skin tissue which we have already discussed. I would kindly ask the Chamber and the Prosecutor, since I received another document later on, to be allowed to quote it only one part, it's another summary. It is marked P1162. Kosovo: Summary report of the French forensic mission, which is the summary for the Cirez site. Perhaps I can quote that from page 6. It says: "The first well is partially filled up with construction debris. In the other two there were floating bodies." If the first well was full of construction debris, then I have no explanation -- or rather, there is only one explanation, which I can think of. If the bodies were thrown in head first how come there were no injuries? These were four female bodies. There were no injuries to the head or on some other parts of the bodies. If they fell in legs first, how come there are no injuries on the lower extremities, on the lower limbs? The only conclusion is, with all due respect for the witness, was that the bodies were lowered into the well rather than thrown in. This is the only way I can think of in terms of explaining the absence of such injuries.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honour, I've been a bit slow to rise on my feet because I was looking for this exhibit. utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, and there is no doubt an opportunity during a coming break for you to have a look at it, but if that is insufficient you will be able to raise the matter. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted to tell Their Honours that we had no particular intention for -- to use this exhibit, although it is related to the 65 ter document, and it does not introduce anything that would be particularly new to the expert report of Professor Stankovic. utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: At the top of the screen in front of you, Mr. Djordjevic, just going off the screen we started with a quotation from the report, which is: "The first well is partially filled up with construction debris." utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC

utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're quite correct, Your Honour, which is confirmed by the witness. The rest were witness's conclusions -- sorry, expert's conclusions.
