utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you were tendering -- what is it that you were tendering? You've given a number. Can you tell us what that is?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Immediately, Your Honour. It is the French forensic medical team in Kosovo in the summer of 1999 Cirez site autopsies K017-6730 to K017-6756. It is 65 ter 00383. This is what the questions put to the witness were about. I believe I had eight questions in total concerning his objections of the findings by his French colleagues in terms of the site in Cirez.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be Exhibit D00924, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. The next topic is P1174. It is the location of Gornja Sudimlja. It is K017-7487, K017-7720. The location, as I said, is Gornja Sudimlja. Again, the French forensic mission in Kosovo, summer of 1999. Could we please see the first page of that report. This is the cover page.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, did you study this as well?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So you had occasion to study the findings of the French forensic mission and their work in Gornja Sudimlja. You could see how they determined the firing distance concerning the projectiles which caused the gun-shot injuries in question. Before directing you to that, can you please explain to us how is range assessed concerning the distance from which projectiles were fired into a body? What methods are possible, and given your years-long experience, sir, what can you tell us about that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: Having analysed the French forensic mission's findings, many things remained clear in my -- unclear in my mind, having in mind the way of interpretation of the range of the barrel before firing, the assessed -- that is why I wanted to refer to the universally accepted principles used in our countries as well as elsewhere concerning gun-shot wounds. Gun-shot wounds can be caused point-blank or from very close range. In such instances the rifle barrel needs to be put against the surface of a body or clothing or up to the distance of 5 millimetres. Such injuries, such gun-shot wounds, are caused -- are called point-blank firing injuries or contact range injuries. Another group would be the injuries caused from close range. It usually occurs with short-barrelled weapons. The barrel cannot be moved by more than 50 centimetres. This indicates that from that distance, if a projectile is fired on the surface of the body and the clothing, one can find gunpowder traces. For example, it can be gunpowder particles, soot, or metal particles. Beyond this distance from 50 centimetres up for short-barrelled weapons and 150 centimetres for long-barrelled weapons, these are distant range injuries. If we have the weapon used to fire at the victim, in such instances there is a comparative analysis that needs to be conducted. In other words, the weapons is used to fire at a pristine surface such as a white sheet of paper and then the type of wound and soot traces are compared to the surface traces in order to determine the distance. In this case, as well as in the analysis of the ballistic experts, I did not find any information about who and how determined the range. I will address that a bit later, specifically the report by the ballistics expert Mr. Pejic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Doctor, can you tell us something about the appearance of the wound in putrefied corpses, and I mean wounds caused by fire-arms with either long or short barrels.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: When one has in mind each of these wounds which were contact-range wounds, they have their specific characteristics. If it's a contact-range distance -- if it's a contact-range injury, then the injury can be circular, oval, or star-shaped if it is in the location where we have large surface bones such as the skull. Gunpowder traces are found inside the wound itself and in the immediate vicinity where they are all of course taken from. In the head area the wound is usually larger. A close- or contact-range injury usually has a circular entry wound with the gunpowder traces circular pattern, and around it there are gunpowder traces, soot, and so on. Distant-range injuries have varying types of shapes. They can be circular, oval, or of another shape depending of the angle. The gunpowder trace ring or circle is different and the traces around the wound are less. These are the main characteristics of such gun-shot wounds. And now about putrefied corpses' injuries. Out of the 5.000 corpses I carried out autopsies on in the war areas, at least three and a half thousand of them had putrefaction changes. This also entails decomposition of parts of body, especially collagen and elastic tissues, binding tissue, and it is impossible to determine with any certainty the profile caused by the fire-arm. If we only make our conclusions based on the shape and type of wound which in the process of putrefaction changes and if that is used only to use the profile, that is to say the calibre of the weapon, then we consider that a professional error; however, I do not see that here. At the same time, I must say, since I wanted to address Mr. Pejic's report -- but this is another document. I don't know if I'm allowed to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I'll stop you here.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have an exhibit next which is P1172, examples 19 and 20. It is page 91 in the B/C/S, and in the English it is 61.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: First I'll have a general question. Without wasting much time on this I wanted to ask you the following: Since in your report you mentioned a number of cases and reasons due to which you were doubtful of the French experts' conclusions, could you please refer to a few cases which you believe are specific or characteristic since I don't think we need to dwell on this topic too much.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, you mentioned page 91.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: If I'm not mistaken, in B/C/S, and this is page 61 in English. This is Exhibit P1172, example 19.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, in the conclusion provided by the forensic experts we can see that "the entry and exit point or wound cannot be identified because of the cranial and facial damage and the loss of bone tissue." However, in the next sentence it is stated that the total appearance suggests that a 12- or 16-millimetre calibre bullet was fired at contact range, so I wonder on the basis of which they made this conclusion. If there was no entry or exit wound, if there was simply destroyed skull, you need to be able to find a trace of gunpowder explosion if you want to make any conclusions of this kind concerning entry and exit wound. So you have to have different particles, gunpowder particles, or anything else in order to be able to draw this type of a conclusion. So I believe that this conclusion does not follow from the report of the forensic experts.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please see the page 121 in B/C/S and page 81 in English of the same document, P1172.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: So this is example 20, if you would kindly continue with your comments.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: On page 121 we have conclusions for the body.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: This is example 20.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: C84, this is small-calibre bullet, so in the same fashion here we can say that the subject had transfacial gun-shot wound, tangential to the skull from right to left, top to bottom, front to back with a low-calibre bullet fired at close range, and so on. And in the description of the wound it is stated that it was impossible to discern neither entry nor exit wound, but the overall appearance suggested that it was a bullet wound, so this conclusion does not follow from the description of the wound. So in this case as well as in some other cases I believe we can say that this was an arbitrary conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please go back to document 1174, P1174, and could we please have page 72 in B/C/S on the screen and page 49 in English. So the exhibit is P1174 and pages are 72 in B/C/S and 49 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: We will wait for a moment to see the document on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So in English it is page 49. The exhibit is 1174.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: So the conclusion number 18, what can you tell us given the depression marks on the skull bones and the mechanism of how they were created, bearing in mind the body L2C68, L2C83, and L2C87? For the sake of the record, I just want to add that this also appears on page 118 in English -- sorry, in B/C/S and 79 in English and on page 130 in B/C/S and 87 in English.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, in the description of this wound we can see that in case of the body L2C67 there was a depression fracture of the skull bone of 6.4 centimetres, and furthermore, it is stated that the cranial trauma caused by a blunt object within the brackets rifle-butt caused the death. As far as I could hear from people who are experts in this, there is no rifle-butt of this diameter. So I fully agreed that this was the description of the wound; however, I don't believe that it was caused by the rifle-butt. Possibly it was another type of blunt object but certainly not a rifle-butt.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Could we now see page 150 in B/C/S and page 101 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Given your objections to the French experts' report, do you believe that this summary is acceptable? Could you please comment on the conclusions that the French expert team drew?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: On the basis of the summary that was provided in this document and bearing in mind everything that I said previously concerning this report, I believe that due to some inconsistencies --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. I said that it was 1174, whereas now we are dealing with Exhibit P1172, page 150 in B/C/S and 101 in English. So it is the document P1172. Go ahead, sir.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: Bearing in mind the conclusion provided by the experts who compiled this report and bearing in mind what I said previously, I believe that a large part of the conclusion of the French forensic expert team is unacceptable from the point of view of forensic medicine, and that is my position which I'm willing to defend here.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now please see the exhibit P1166, pages 26 in B/C/S, one part of the relevant text is on page 27 as well, and we have the same pages in English, that is, page 26 and 27. As I said, it was Exhibit P1166.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: My question for you, sir, has to do with a topic that is also covered on pages 40 in B/C/S and in English. Sir, you can see the cover page here. Have you seen this report before?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I analysed this report from the point of view of my speciality, and bearing in mind everything that is mentioned here by the ballistic expert who compiled this report - and that report was used to determine the distances from which the projectiles were fired. So the ballistic expert says: "It should be noted that the profiles were taken during firing tests carried out using 10 per cent ballistic gelatin. Now this mixture is a simulant of even consistency that mimics muscle at rest." On a body we do not register entry wounds on muscle tissue but rather, on skin tissue, and the competition of the skin tissue is rather different from the composition of the muscle tissue. At the same time here, they're saying that the gelatin mimics the muscle at rest, and we know that obviously at any moment in time when somebody's wounded somebody can see the person firing at him or who can see the gun-shots, then such persons are trying to hide or run away, so they're not at rest. So obviously we have three layers of the skin, epidermis, the upper layer; dermis, which is the middle layer; and deep layer as well, and each of these three layers is composed of different cells. So in the deep layer we have a great number of elastic fibres, but we also have nerve fibres and different other fibres that provide elasticity. We also have the binding tissue and -- whereas on the upper layer we have epithelial cells which serve as protection. So you cannot use this particular test to draw any certain conclusions concerning the profiles and calibres of guns that were used to inflict certain wounds. We said already that we had dead bodies that were all in an advanced stage of decomposition, and this putrefaction caused certain changes in the composition of the body in the majority of cases and increase of wounds which was also decision of the gases that appear within the chest as a result of putrefaction, so I believe that the conclusions of the kind that were drawn by these ballistic experts are unacceptable. We tried in the military medical academy to do the same thing using the ballistic gelatin, and we also tried -- we also tried to use paraffin cast and fire at that because we believed that this was the closest to the body. We also wanted to use tests on animals, but we couldn't proceed with that. We had to reduce them because we had protests from different NGOs fighting for animal rights. So we looked at the tests carried out by our Norwegian colleagues to see how they did it within the scope of a project of co-operation, and possibly if you made tests of that kind you could draw some relevant conclusions. But I believe that the conclusions drawn by this ballistic expert are unacceptable.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now please see on the screen exhibit P1165. This is another report of the French forensic mission carried out in summer of 1999 in Kosovo in the site of Izbica.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, these are autopsies K017-976 -- 6652. So could we please, first of all, see the cover page of this document, P1165. Sir, could you please tell me whether you considered this report when you compiled your report, so this report of the French forensic mission in Kosovo for the Izbica site.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. But if you allow me to add just one sentence to what I was saying before, and that is that the conclusion of that ballistic expert report which is on page 41 of the document we could previously see was that in Gornja Sudimlja site all the shots were fired at point-blank range or with guns leaning against the body, which is contrary to the majority of conclusions or the majority of finds that we could see in the French forensic experts' report. Because in those findings this conclusion could not be drawn because the conclusion is that these were all fired at point-blank range; in other words, that these were executions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now see page 2 of this document in B/C/S. In English it is page 3. Thank you. I also need to say that the relevant pages are also page 19 in B/C/S, which is page 14 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: What could you tell us concerning the difference between people allegedly killed and the number of cartridges that were found on the site?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: In this report it is stated that approximately 150 persons were killed, and later on on page 19 and 20 we can see that 84 fragments of war munition were recovered. If every single body only got one gun-shot wound and this doesn't follow from this report, then we could say that more than one-half of these persons had gun-shot wounds, whereas the rest of them didn't have any. So we have a great difference between the number of cartridges and the number of wounds. If all the cartridges were found on the same spot, then we could conclude that the number of persons allegedly killed does not correspond to what the finding suggests.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now please see page 7 in B/C/S and page 5 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, here you can see the description of damaged clothes. Can we talk about the distance from which the projectiles were fired?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: In the description on damage to the male clothing, ISD1E1 it says: Holes in the upper third of the back indicate that this was a point-blank range firing. They do not say whether any fire traces were found on the clothing or whether -- whether there were any traces of gunpowder explosion on the fabric. So based on what they made this conclusion is not clear at all. They say that the fabric was damaged from its edge, but they do not describe the damage, which is much more important, how this jacket was damaged and whether it was done from -- by firing from close -- or rather, point-blank range.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now see page 20 in B/C/S and page 15 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Our question for you: How can one determine the calibre, and is it possible to do that on the basis of damage on fabric, on clothes?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: If we have a fabric that has holes diameter 29 millimetres and then based on that they conclude that it was 12-millimetre calibre, then one has to wonder: How did they conclude this and on the basis of which parameters? If we know that this fabric was also in the soil for some period of time and that fabric is also susceptible to changes and decomposition, then such a finding would be considered faulty and our courts would reject it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now see page 22 in B/C/S and 16 in English in the same document.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: We can see the conclusion of the French forensic mission here. Can you please comment on their conclusion.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't want anyone to misunderstand me. It's hard to discuss somebody's finding when the author is not there and you cannot confront him and challenge his opinion. I would really like some of the authors of this report to explain to us based on what they reached this conclusion without having autopsy findings of the victims and that the clothing was as described here, torn and decomposed due to spending some time in the soil and so on. Based on the description of the clothing given here and analysed, one cannot reach these conclusions, these findings. I don't want to use any heavy language, but to put it mildly it's unacceptable. We do not have any description of traces indicating that around these openings there are traces of blood. We know that putrid fluid can come out of various cavities, but not from parts of the human body where the skin is preserved. So I would like to know based on which data they came to such a conclusion, and I would like to face the authors of this author [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: And what is your comment on this finding?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: As I've already said, this finding is unacceptable.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, while preparing for this testimony and also earlier, you had a chance to see video marked as --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters didn't hear the number of the video.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But it is Exhibit P288. I will not ask that that video be played now.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: But given that you saw this video excerpt, I would like to ask you to comment on it in relation to the findings in the expert report of the French forensic team in relation to the bodies that we discussed so far in the Izbica location.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: I watched this video excerpt on a number of occasions, which you can see in my expert report. Also, having analysed material from Izbica and statements, I could determine that these people perished in three locations. However, the video footage one can see corpses and when one analyses the area and the appearance of the corpses, one can see that the corpses had been found in nine locations. First, one body wrapped in a blanket was found in a warehouse with quartermaster items there. And then number 2, we have bodies lined up on a green meadow. This is 6 minutes, 26 seconds into the excerpt, and one can see that the bodies had been brought in from elsewhere because on the soles of their footwear there were layers of mud while the meadow surface is clean. Then there was one body with a large stomach and characteristic clothes seen 9 minutes and 10 seconds into the footage. This body is seen again 36 minutes, 18 seconds into the video excerpt, and this body is brought on a tractor-trailer for burial. Then we can see bodies in a low bitter oak forest 11 minutes, 10 seconds into the film. And then on a meadow with burn damage and intact tractors 6 minutes, 5 seconds into the film. And then there are bodies lined up next to each other by a low bitter oak forest. Then there is a body lying on a yellowish blanket, 18 minutes, 20 seconds into the film. Six bodies with pieces of paper on their chests bearing the family Bajra and various other names, 26 minutes, 2 seconds into the film. Bodies brought on blankets, one wearing a green camouflage uniform 20 minutes, 30 seconds into the footage. And so on. So based on this film one can see that the bodies were found in more than three locations.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The next clip, the next footage, can you tell us whether this footage can be used as evidence on the number and type of injuries?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not prone to challenging despite the impression that you may have had so far, I'm not prone to challenging what is -- what can be found in various exhibits. But this footage can be used as evidence if later on it is supported by autopsy reports for these corpses. In this particular case we cannot compare this footage to the autopsy reports that were done by, say, Dr. Tomasevic. If we were to compare the bodies we can see in this film with at least some of the visible injuries on the head and compare that to the autopsy reports of Dr. Tomasevic and the description contained therein, then that could be confirmed. But in that particular case it was not done. So based on the report of Dr. Tomasevic we see that all bodies received gun-shot wounds. In one case they describe a body whose nose was broken, and then after that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Could you pause here, please, Doctor.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honour, the comments of this witness regarding Dr. Tomasevic are on page 12 of the report. Pursuant to Your Honours' decision issued this week, that portion of the report has been redacted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That's why I interrupted the doctor, Mr. Djordjevic. I think this is dealing with a part of his report that is not received in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is correct, Your Honours. As a result of that we redacted the first version, and we took out the report of Dr. Tomasevic, in compliance with the Court order, even though this report pertains to Izbica, and so far it was not admitted into evidence. The Defence did intend to tender it into evidence, but naturally we cannot oppose the Court order. And as a result of that, we redacted the initial version, and our witness didn't know this and he started commenting on Dr. Tomasevic's report. So naturally we cannot continue with this line of questioning. I don't think there's anything bad in him mentioning Dr. Tomasevic's report, but we will stop it here. This is 65 ter 00248. That's the report of Dr. Tomasevic on the autopsy results from Izbica, summer 1999, which is precisely the topic of the work of the French forensic team. May I continue, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes. Please move on. For the reasons indicated we won't be considering this part of the evidence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have a statement by Milazim Thaqi. This is D126. And it's in evidence, page 5, please. In both B/C/S and English, paragraph 1 in English of that statement. We have a document that we would be tendering into evidence. These are some photographs, and the Prosecution has been notified of this, but let us first look at page 5 in B/C/S and page 5, paragraph 1 in English --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Before that, Ms. Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honour, I rise to my feet simply because this witness statement is again a statement that is not dealt within the report of the witness. He has no comments on this specifically, and it is our position that he shouldn't be allowed to comment on a statement that has not been directly addressed within his report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's an identical situation as the statement of the previous witness. A very short comment concerning what is stated in that statement, which will be supported by the photographs which are Prosecution's exhibit. This is why Defence yesterday asked for additional time to prepare for this. So could we please see Exhibit 126, page 5 in B/C/S and 5 in English, paragraph 1. And immediately --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Before you rush ahead, Mr. Djordjevic, there is an objection. The Chamber, though, as it did with the last objection, with they being very similar, would allow you to continue with this. So that having been done, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I apologise for the fact that the Defence seems to be impatient.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 1. You have seen this statement, you have gone over it, haven't you, Dr. Stankovic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now see the photographs, please, 65 ter 227. The Prosecution has been notified of this, 65 ter 227. Could we see them after this.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: We saw what is stated here. You will now see the photographs. And please tell us, what are possible interpretations. Have you read this?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please show us the photographs, 65 ter 227.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Just pause a minute, please, Mr. Djordjevic. We have no English on the screen at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I missed that, Your Honours. The same page, page 5 in English. So both in B/C/S and in English, page 5. In English it's paragraph 1. D126, page 5.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: No, that's B/C/S again, Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We saw the English text. I'm convinced that there is an English version, but if the Trial Chamber allows, I can read it out slowly in B/C/S rather than wait like we did last time, 3 to 5 minutes. Would you allow me to read it in B/C/S, Your Honours, and then it will be interpreted for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: If we are waiting it is because the reference you've given is not accurate, but please read it slowly in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. "The machine-gun fired endlessly, and two men fell on my back and knocked me down on the ground. Both of them fell over me. One was my relative Uke Uka, 74 years old from Broja. The upper part of his head was blown apart and his brains dispersed all over me. He fell over my upper body and over my right shoulder. The other man was Isuf Zezeqa Shala, 63 years old from Broja. He fell over my upper body on the left side and over my shoulder. The shooting went on for just several seconds, and it seemed to me that the policemen who had escorted us fired because I didn't he see any other policemen near us. He sprayed bullets all over us three times up and down. The bullets flew all around me and some of them zoomed past my head, but I wasn't hit. Later on I saw three bullet-holes on the back of my jacket, sweater, and shirt. It seems that the bullets have come from the side and just grazed my back. I'm fortunate to be alive. God protected me he." Could we now see photographs. As I said, it's 65 ter 227. One by one, please. This is the jacket -- or the shirt the witness mentioned. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Doctor, did you have an opportunity to view these photographs?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I think they are of poor quality, too poor, actually, to be able to draw any conclusions. However, I need to comment on the statement itself, if I am allowed to do so. If someone had one or two bodies on the back and the locations of bullet-holes are specified, such damage to his clothing could not have occurred. It could only have happened if the person was standing and if fired at laterally. In that case, having in mind the size of the back, there must have been soft tissue damage or wounds to the ribs which would be followed by bleeding, and that would have left marks on the clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will provide the English reference. It is D126. The B/C/S was 0301-3042 and the English is 1600-0118. Before that we have IC 1600-0118 and 0301-3042, as I've said already. Thank you. This was the other part that Defence wanted to tender, and it was redacted pursuant to your instruction. The next document is P1139.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Was there anything else you wanted to tell us about Izbica, Doctor, before we move on to the report of Dr. Eric Baccard?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: I could perhaps mention --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Without mentioning, though.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: Without mentioning, that we also have in mind witness statements, and the findings of Dr. Tomasevic is something I cannot comment upon. Yes, I'll follow your instruction of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Although the doctor said that the photographs are poor, we still would like to have them admitted to serve as evidence, Your Honours. This is 65 ter 227. This is on the Prosecutor's list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: They will be received as one exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be Exhibit D00925, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. The next topic we wanted to deal with is P1139. Forensic medical analysis and summary of reports in forensic examinations conducted in Kosovo in 1999 by Dr. Eric Baccard. It is K021-4664 and K021-4817. Could we please have page 9 in the B/C/S and in the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: You can see it in your documents, Doctor. Did you have occasion to view this analysis?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. There's a conclusion stated that each location was covered by the same method of forensic examination. This was a summary of the analysis of Dr. Baccard. Do you agree with this statement when medical/legal examinations are used as applied by different teams from Switzerland, Finland, Belarus, Serbia, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: It is a bit odd that after so many investigations, which were done upon the request of this Prosecutor's office and in Bosnia as well as in Croatia and in other locations where there were consequences of the war, that the method determined for the investigation of mass graves, including the methodology by Mr. Wright, who's an Australian, as well as a number of cases where I took part in be it as Prosecution or Defence witness that I was able to observe, it is rather odd that in this area a different methodology was used. As indicated in the first sentence, it goes against the grain of the rest of the report when it states that the used methodology was identical. If you use the method used by the French mission headed by Lecomte, you can see that there are drastic differences in terms of approach to autopsy as well as manner of description and to the contents of such autopsy reports. I don't think it was the same methodology.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Could you single out any of the applied methodologies as specific?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I might be biassed in that and misunderstood, but I believe that the colleagues from the medical forensic institute in Belgrade created such detailed reports that one can learn anything and everything in terms of interest of investigative organs from those reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This related to the methods. What about the overall report of Dr. Baccard, what can you say about that in general terms as you provided it in your report?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: Reading the report I was minded to provide my own opinion on some of his findings; however, first I wanted to address the end of the summary report. This report contains 158 pages. Nine pages are the contents. Three pages is the CV of Mr. Baccard. 83 pages contain summaries of autopsy reports of the corpses in the locations of Racak, Bela Crkva, Mala Krusa, Djakovica; in two streets, Padalista, Izbica, Kotlina, Dubrava, Vata, Stagovo, Gornja Sudimlja, the prison in Dubrava, the cemetery in Rakos and Suva Reka. All those reports amounted to 83 pages. As for the notes by Dr. Baccard, they cover 63 pages. For all of the reports, so it is one person going through the reports, drafted 63 pages of remarks. From a forensic point of view, if he concludes that all those remarks do not amount to any significant changes to the opinions provided by the experts previously, then I have no comment. If there were so many remarks or objections they should have been dealt with, with the teams working on the autopsies. It should be worked out between them and Dr. Baccard. There are examples, if I may, which I can quote, and I referred to them in my expert report. Do you want me to be specific? But, for example, have a look at page 101. I quote: "The description of two entry and two exit wounds, that's a remark. This was done by those who carried out the autopsy." Then it says: "During X-ray examination, it was ascertained that there were four bullets." This is a disastrous professional error. This is impermissible. It is JBG 35/SR, page 10.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Please stop, Professor, for the sake of our friends from the Prosecution and the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What the doctor referred to was page 101, but in the English version it is page 88. Could we please have that on the screen so that everyone can see it. First page 101 and then page 104.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Is this what you were talking about?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. The next page is 104 in the B/C/S spills over to page 105, and the English is page 91. What is this, Doctor?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: These are the discrepancies between Dr. Baccard and the autopsy team and their findings at Padalista. He states the following remarks: "In all cases the date of death is wrong. No specific methodology is referred to." Next, wrong victim information. For example, Mihanc Imeraj it says 19 years old in the report; and Mihanc Imeraj, 70 years of age in the schedule -- 72 years of age. Feride Imeraj in the report, 8 years old; and then Feride Imeraj, 21 years old in schedule E. Sabahat Imeraj, a female in the report; and Sabahat Imeraj, a male in schedule E. Raba Imeraj female in the report; and Rab Imeraj, a male in schedule E, and Fatime Salibaj does not figure in schedule E or appendix E.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Page 90.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: But there is one more thing. Concerning Arijeta Imeraj [phoen], the pathologist in the report states that the upper limbs were amputated, and in the conclusions the reference is made to only one. This is concerning Dr. Baccard's remarks.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Page 90 -- sorry, 107 in the B/C/S and 93 in the English, the same document of course.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: This is the forensic analysis --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Wait a minute, Doctor, let's wait for it to be put on the screen. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: In the summary Dr. Baccard states: "The limited nature of this research is the result of poor quality of the images obtained from this videotape whose definition is very imperfect and does not allow an important enlargement of the details." Next he says that: "It is for these reasons that no finding can be deemed reliable. Only diagnostic assumptions can be taken into account." As far as I know, one cannot base evidence on assumptions. This should not be accepted as such.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Next could we have page 25 in the B/C/S and 23 in the English. We'll wait for the system. This is Racak, that part of Dr. Baccard's report. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Doctor, what can you tell us about the cause of death of the bodies in Racak?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: The report speaks of 40 bodies which were found and later on analysed and that come from Racak; whereas, this report speaks of 64 causes of death, that is to say, that 40 persons have 64 causes of death. One person can have only one cause of death, but not one and a half causes of death. They cannot die from this and from that and have it portrayed as this. So this is one illogical conclusion which is not the only one by no means. I remember that there was a similar situation in Srebrenica where for 2.082 corpses there were 2700 causes of death. So this kind of findings is unacceptable and illogical.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now see page 27 in B/C/S and page 25 in English, same document.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: How do you interpret the location of gun-shot wounds, or rather, locations of entry wounds in the bodies found in Racak?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: Based on the location of these wounds, one can speak of a situation in which people who perished in Racak found -- were perished in the area because this type of wounds that came from front and back and from left and from right could only have been -- come under these circumstances. I don't see a particular problem, bearing in mind that such injuries are frequent with people who take part in combat.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: And what is your conclusion?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: Without knowing any other information, witness statements and so on, such injuries could have been inflicted on persons who were surrounded and not persons who were executed only.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, something about the paraffin test, which is supposed to establish the presence of gunpowder particles. You saw in the report that they did the paraffin test on the bodies found in Racak. So please tell us about that method and about the findings in -- from Racak.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: The paraffin test is normally performed by forensic technicians and investigative organs in order to determine the presence of traces of gunpowder explosion on the hands and palms in order to prove that there are gunpowder traces there which had not burnt, and that enables us to establish whether the person on whom the paraffin test was done fired from a weapon or not. This paraffin glove test is done in all countries, and the analysis of this test in our area is done with concentrated sulfur acid and another chemical which are used to prove the presence of certain chemicals. This method is not completely reliable, and it can give positive results in all situations where a hand comes into contact with a certain chemical. This is why this test is considered not entirely reliable, and I think that back in 1968 at the Interpol congress it was said that this test is one of auxiliary methods that can be used to prove the presence of gunpowder particles but is not completely reliable. The analysis with an electronic microscope is the only acceptable method and the only safe method that can prove the presence of unburnt gunpowder particles. In our particular case we used the paraffin test with concentrated sulfur acid and another chemical, but as I said, it is not a completely reliable test, and if we do have a positive finding, that is not certain yet that the person did, in fact, fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know on how many bodies this test was performed? Can you give us any conclusions concerning that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't have findings on that issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Doctor, how did you see that there was a body without a head?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: Based on the summaries that one saw in evidence, it doesn't follow that there was a single body that was headless. I have to reiterate that in all cases in bodies of Racak the cause of death was linked to gun-shot wounds. However, there is a sentence indicating that in about 20 per cent of bodies there were visible traces of post mortem activity of animals, but there are no descriptions, further descriptions, concerning this. So all I can say is what I have just told you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to put another question before we make our break. It's page 96, 97, 98, and 99 in B/C/S, and pages 83, 84, 85, and 86 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Are there significant discrepancies or differences in the findings of Serbian and Ukrainian pathologists on the one hand and the Finnish pathologists report when it comes to findings from Racak?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: There are two types of discrepancies: One is acceptable and one isn't. The discrepancies are differences of cause of death can be found in 16 cases. I don't think that this is a major discrepancy or a major difference. For example, if we look at 6-7023F in the Finnish report it is stated that the cause of death is the fracture of aorta and the bleeding that resulted in the chest. The Serbian team said something very very similar, although it was phrased in different terms. So I don't think that that's a major difference or a major discrepancy. However, there is another kind of differences or discrepancies which is significant, and that is the one in the description of gun-shot wounds and their number on the bodies of victims, and it exists in 11 cases, as many as 11. Given that both these teams were present on the site, they should have given their joint opinion or joint finding on this, including this discrepancy in the number of wounds on bodies which is quite significant. It is not up to me now to say who was right, but this is a significant discrepancy that exists in these two reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Before we break I would like to bring to your attention that there is a mistake in the transcript. It shouldn't be Serbian and Russian team rather than -- it should be Serbian and Belarus, Belorussian team, so not -- it should be Serbian and Belorussian team. Now could we see 54 -- or P524 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... time. Can this wait until after the break?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well. We'll have the second break now and resume at five minutes past 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: While we wait for the witness, could I mention one matter. During the break a consideration was being given to the written submissions about the admissibility of a video. The DVD with which we've been presented discloses only a few very short clips, whereas the submissions in part at least are dealing with a video of some 30 minutes of length. Can it be clear what it is that is being tendered, whether it is just the short clips or the full video, and is the -- if it's only the short clips, is the Chamber to have regard to the whole video for the purpose of assessing, for example, some of the Defence objections that it's clearly inconsistent in photography and location and so forth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I mention that now. You may need to think about it and please confirm at a later time if you're not ready to confirm now just what is intended. But at the moment there's an inconsistency between what we're offered as the exhibit and the submissions and our understanding of what it was about. Thank you. If you could continue, Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. [Interpretation] Could we please see Exhibit P454, the title page of this report. P454. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Doctor, have you had an occasion to review this report?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I reviewed this report too.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I will first ask you whether by examining this report, did you also have a chance to see the CV of Jose Pablo-Baraybar?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I had the occasion to review his CV.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As you also hold an academic title, do you know that there is an exam in the studies of archaeology that has something to do with medical education. Did you notice in Jose Pablo-Baraybar's CV the information that he took a part of the exam that had to do with medical knowledge apart from archaeology?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: On the basis of this section of CV which is admitted into evidence, it turns out that he did not take a single medical exam while he was studying archaeology at a social sciences faculty.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now please see page 3 of this document in B/C/S and also page 3 in the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: This is what it looks like in e-court. On the hard copy the number is lower, it's page 2. In the paper copy that you have but in e-court we have page 3 both in B/C/S and English. Does forensic anthropology require some sort of medical knowledge?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: From this material I will quote something from page 2, a section that says: "Therefore, forensic anthropology applies the medically based study of the human skeleton's development in the legally oriented contents of the criminal proceedings." What follows from this is that dealing with forensic anthropology implies the necessary university level medical education. From what Mr. Baraybar has written, that's what follows from that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please see page 9 in B/C/S and page 9 in English as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, once again we see some assumptions here as well as some conclusions. Can you give us a comment on this.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: In this part of the report it says, I'm quoting: "It is assumed that the gun-shot wound happened at the moment of death. This is why this is considered to be the cause of death." As I said earlier, no single proof can be based on assumption but on material traces. This way of understanding and interpreting things like gun-shot wounds and cause of death is something that is unacceptable.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: All right. If we look at page 2 -- page 8 of the same document, I think it's the same in both languages, please have a look at what is stated about the cause of death, the injury of the shoulder or of the thigh bone. Can you just briefly comment on that.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it follows from the previous conclusion. It says that the gun-shot wound which caused complex injuries to the body, the shoulder wound, the humerus and femur would have compromised the brachial and femoral arteries leading to death following severe blood loss." We know from experience that the injuries to the femur and humerus by gun-shot wounds do not always necessarily cause injury to brachial and femoral arteries. So it's another assumption which is not founded on medical knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Could we please see page 11 in both versions. Please let us wait for the English text to appear. Could you please comment as you have commented here about the establishing of the causes of death done by Serbian forensic experts and the OMPF as Mr. Baraybar was at the head of this.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: From these reports of forensic teams and the conclusions which forensic medical experts have drawn, one can see, at least in my opinion, and also judging by what is usually done in our country, is that many of them would go within the remit of work of a judge or the prosecutor's office. It seems that at every moment they're trying to say what they're not requested to say and what they're not certain about. Things such as the cause of death and everything else connected with the death of a person after the examination of forensic medical experts is something that he should describe. When there are elements to say something decidedly, he is obliged to do that. However, if a forensic medical expert only receives mortal remains in which he can register certain injuries to the bones but there is no soft tissue anymore as these are bodies in which during the putrefaction the soft tissue has been lost, then the person in question can only express his opinion on what has been found. On the basis of all the other materials such as the statements of witnesses and criminal technical examination and so on, the truth is to be established. But I think that here these kind of conclusions are not acceptable. It is the sort of attitude that I could not support at any expert meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please see page 12 in both languages now, though a part of the English text overflows onto page 13. But let's see page 12 in both versions first, please, let's just wait briefly. We have it in B/C/S now, and here it is in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: How do you interpret the lack of correspondence between the opinion of the Serbian forensic experts and the OMPF experts in the case of the body of Ba-12, that's Lirie Berisha?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: I think that one of the shortcomings of the forensic experience contributes to the fact that some of the injuries are interpreted, let me not say arbitrarily, but on the basis of what other people do or what we saw or didn't see. In this specific case I would ask for these parts of a skull to be shown --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we could see page 13 in the English, please, we can see these parts of the skull. Should we zoom in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can use this one and then we shall see.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Can you please zoom in the photos, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: In this photograph we can see the bones of the base of the skull, and in the area of the back of the head you can see a bone defect which the -- those who were doing the autopsy they described it in their report. They mentioned the diameter, and they claimed that it was an injury caused by a projectile and that it looks like a keyhole. If we know that the so-called keyhole injury's caused when a -- in the bones of the roof of the skull primarily in the section where the bones are protruding, then we can see what they say here. Where does this projectile go when it leaves the skull? This is what we can see in the left parietal area. So if we take the spine then this is maybe 7 or 8 centimetres from the surface of soft tissues in the neck. So therefore the injury in the soft tissues which are described here would have to be there; however, this injury has not been registered. There should also be the injury to the vertebra and considering that it moves from left to the right and from the back to the right simultaneously and that's not here. Then the defect -- the injury's also described as having the shape, as you can see, and as one can calculate as there is a special technique used for that, that it is 4 and a half centimetres long and up to 0.6 centimetres wide. I'm not sure what sort of projectile could cause this kind of damage or this kind of bone defect. If we also see that the bones of the roof of the skull, that a defect in the bones is also registered there and that its diameter is 9.5 by 7.5 centimetres and that in these sections of the bones damage caused by fire has also been registered, then it seems quite certain that this injury was caused in some different manner. In such a situation I believe that the opinions should be harmonised because this is a typical example, and then leave it to those carrying out the autopsy, the forensic experts, to have a conference and then try to settle this dilemma. In my opinion, this is not a keyhole injury, considering that the head was burnt, that the area where the mortal remains were found included traces of projectiles that were never shot. It's possible that there was an explosion and that some of the hard materials or traces of projectiles did cause this sort of injury, but in any case, I do not think that this is the keyhole wound or a gun-shot wound, considering everything that I have just stated.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. My next question has to do with page 15 in B/C/S and page 17 in the English version, so could we please see them on the screen. My question is: What is your opinion when you compare the gun-shot wounds in bodies that were exhumed in Serbia with those who were killed, for example, we can see the Afghanistan, Cambodia, or the Gulf War? What is this about, Doctor, can you please comment on this?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the war conflict in the territory of Kosovo was significantly different in character from the war conflict in Afghanistan, Cambodia, or the Gulf War, considering the weapons that were used in the respective territories. In the territories that are discussed here, Cambodia, Afghanistan, and the Gulf War, heavy weaponry was used. In the armed conflicts in Kosovo, the only weapons which were used were hand-held fire-arms and also mines and explosives which belonged to the police. Under such circumstances, considering that the selection of weapons was limited, sometimes these were hand-held mortars, then I don't think it is instructive to compare such wars and the injuries sustained by people in these territories with those who were killed in Kosovo primarily because of the different weapons used in these conflicts.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have D64 put on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Doctor, have you seen this report?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have page 3 in the B/C/S and in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Please look at the conclusion in which there is a link made between the injuries and cause of death. What do you think of these conclusions?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: I think I've provided an answer already concerning the previous report, and this is reflected in that document as well. To me this is unacceptable. It is based on a presumption. It says: "Due to the impossibility of determining whether gun-shot injuries had been inflicted immediately prior to or after the death of the victim, it was assumed that the gun-shot injuries occurred at the time of death and therefore contributed to it. Any other assumption would have made the examination of the remains totally meaningless." This is contrary to what I was taught. In my view, this is an impermissible way to draw a conclusion such as this.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we go to page 10, please, in the B/C/S and 9 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, again we have rib injuries. I wanted to hear your comment about the mechanism of such injuries.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: It says here that the rib fractures could have been caused by direct impact or pressure exercised on the rib-cage. I agree with that. However, I also must say that such injuries can also occur after a fall on a blunt and uneven object or surface at the location where the body was found or where the injury occurred. I must say that annually I provide expert opinion in about 400 cases. For the most part it has to do with traffic accidents. Such indirect injuries, i.e., rib fractures, can also be seen in cases of impact which needn't necessarily be a direct impact but, for example, can occur during a crash between two vehicles or between a vehicle and a pedestrian. So one needs to add to this that such rib injuries could have been caused by falling and hitting blunt and uneven objects and surfaces.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we go to page 12 in the B/C/S and 11 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Doctor, please give us your opinion on the conclusions arrived at by your colleagues -- I apologise, by Mr. Baraybar and his team concerning the fractures.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: In that part of the report it says: "Injuries to ribs and to the tibia as well as the lower leg occurred sometime before death, as demonstrated by the presence of reactive new bone formation." In my book it means that there was a fracture registered which occurred a few days before death. Then the presence of new bone formation associated with the injuries indicates post traumatic survival and it is, therefore, suggested that the injuries were not inflicted to kill but to persecute the victims. What is this founded on? What is this based on? This is completely arbitrary. For new bone formation to come about, for a bone to begin healing, time is required. It takes at least ten days to be able to observe this new bone formation or scalus [phoen] as expertly referred to. If there had been an injury, a fracture on this person and then that person was kept for another ten days before he or she was killed and if no medical assistance was given, then one needs to have further proof of that. Otherwise, to conclude a thing like that forensically and medically speaking is impermissible.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we he have page 22 in the B/C/S and 19 in the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: This is case number 12000/0256. Just below the picture we see it says figure 6a probable gun-shot wound through left scapula. He we'll see that. And on page 24 in the B/C/S, since we already saw these bone fragments, and page 21 in the English, it is stated that the cause of death were multiple gun-shot wounds to the chest and pelvis. Can you comment?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I may bore everyone if I repeat yet again that a conclusion must come from what was previously stated in the findings. In this case the findings describe something else. It says "probable gun-shot injury," and after that without any hedge whatsoever it is stated that the multiple gun-shot wounds to the chest and pelvis were the cause of death.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 28 in the B/C/S and 25 in the English next. Let's wait for the one in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Here we have an injury to the denture -- to the dentition as well as everything that refers to case NN 8 1000. Can you please comment.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: It is claimed here that the broken or damaged dentition occurred in a number of the teeth and that there was axial loading through the mandible by which the upper and lower teeth impacted against a hard object put into the mouth, which is what caused these fractures. This probably occurred ante mortem. This also needs further proof. If there was a hard object in the mouth which was placed between the teeth, and then if someone was hitting the soft tissues, specifically upper and lower jaw, then there must have been injuries to the soft tissue, such as bruises or abrasions on the skin, which are otherwise not observed if there are no soft tissues. However, since there is only a thin layer of soft tissue such bruises spread and can be clearly visible because they would cover and colour the area of the lower jaw or the upper jaw. It is only in such a case a conclusion as this could be valid. Otherwise, this is not based on any material evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now have P799.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, para 1 of this page of your report is on page 16 in the English and 20 of your hard copy report. This paragraph 1 was deleted. Please do bear in mind that. We'll skip this part since it was redacted. Let's wait for the next page of the document. Did you have an opportunity to see this?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 20 in the B/C/S and 17 in the English, please, of this document. This is Antonio Alonso in the B/C/S, please, as well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Is the number of autopsies of mortal remains identical to the number of those identified by DNA analysis? I have in mind the findings between K048-5493 to K048-5519, page 1. I think you know what I am referring to.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: There is a drastic difference between the number of the allegedly -- of the alleged bodies for which autopsies were carried out for which the experts determined that were the mortal remains of 55 individuals. However, DNA analysis indicated that this number was not as great, or rather, that there were only 41 persons. This is rather embarrassing for those who worked on the bodies of the victims.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Are there any other conclusions concerning this, Professor?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: The difference, the discrepancy, between the number of individuals is something which is indicative of the corpse examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: What does it speak of?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it may bring into question the expertise of the people involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can people whose mortal remains who were never located be considered war victims solely on the basis of witness statements?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: I must say that under our circumstances one needs to be realistic and careful about that. I cannot remember the name of a person whose name is on the monument in Srebrenica. In any case, six or seven years later that same person was found alive in Sremska Mitrovica living and working there. Then Amida Sevdic [phoen] who was born on 7 January 1972 in Skelani near Srebrenica allegedly went missing on the 12th of July, 1995, on her way from Srebrenica to Tuzla. However, nowadays she lives in Arilje as Slavica Stefanovic, and by decision of the basic court in Srebrenica dated the 20th of February, 2008 she was declared dead. There are other examples like that, but I believe that in such circumstances as those prevailing in the territory of the former Yugoslavia one needs to be very careful when pronouncing anyone a war victim and when there are no mortal remains involved. Of course such a person should be considered as someone who had gone missing in the war. There was also the case of Slobodan Letica, a person who was killed in a traffic accident in Vukovar in 1996 -- sorry, in 1986. He then allegedly became a war victim in Vukovar in 1991. We submitted a report which the UN later on marked as their own about that very issue. There are other examples like that. All this needs to be kept in mind. I also quoted the findings from Padalista, where they verified that there was a victim who subsequently did not have his or her name included on the victims list.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. My last question concerning your report: Did you notice the use of certain terms or lingo which is not in keeping with the professional terminology concerning the report by Antonio Alonso?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: There is a word "massacre" mentioned in his report, which is not to be used by geneticist and molecular biologists because this is not a topic of their research. It was used in some preliminary documents and in the report itself, which is, to a certain extent, acceptable having in mind the role of a biogeneticists in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this concludes our examination-in-chief of expert Stankovic. We would like to thank him for coming here to discuss his report before the Chamber. We also seek to tender his report into evidence, the redacted version. It is D011-5432. To repeat, it was redacted pursuant to your -- Their Honours instructions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Djordjevic. That report will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This would be Exhibit D00926, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Doctor, we have to adjourn now because another court uses this courtroom in the afternoon, so we must continue tomorrow morning at 9.00. A court officer will assist you out, and we look forward to continuing your evidence tomorrow morning. We now adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
